issues.what_happened: The ALLOCATOR changed the initial allocation (beds 19/33/20/24 to 18/32/19/27, nurses 8/12/9/8 to 8/11/9/9). Simulations of both show zero overflow and identical nurse coverage in every department and level.
issues.what_should_have_happened: Keep the reference allocation, since the move gave no measurable benefit.
issues.why_incorrect: Reallocation tau was non-zero but the same patients were bedded and every department had the same covered need. The explanation itself says the outcomes are identical.
issues.impact: None on patients. The move was later undone, see the day 3 reversals.
issues.corrective_action: Only reallocate when a measurable gain exists.

issues.what_happened: Nurses were set to 9/12/9/7. A split such as 8/12/9/8 gives the same level 3 and level 2 coverage and more level 1 coverage. Chosen covered about 35.5 against about 35.55. The chosen split left level 1 shortage of 0.15 in IM and 0.15 in orthopedics, and wasted 0.9 of a nurse in cardiology.
issues.what_should_have_happened: Use a split with less level 1 shortage, for example 8/12/9/8, which gives a 0.25 total shortage instead of 0.3.
issues.why_incorrect: A better whole-number split of the same pool existed (equal on levels 3 and 2, better overall). The explanation presents the shortage as unavoidable.
issues.principle: Efficiency, nurse coverage in level order.
issues.impact: About 0.05 nurse-equivalents of level 1 need left uncovered avoidably.
issues.corrective_action: Search integer splits for the best coverage in level order.

issues.what_happened: Cardiology +3 beds and orthopedics -3 beds undo the day 1 moves (cardiology -1, orthopedics +3).
issues.what_should_have_happened: Avoid moves that reverse recent moves.
issues.why_incorrect: Units of tau undone within 3 days: cardiology 1 unit, orthopedics 3 units.

issues.impact: Churn. Cardiology went 18, 21, 18, 22 beds over days 2 to 5.
issues.corrective_action: Use demand trends to avoid oscillation.

issues.what_happened: IM -1 nurse undoes the day 4 gain of +1.
Cardiology +2 nurses undoes the day 4 cut of -2.

The current allocation leaves 3 level-2 patients waiting in neurology and 1 in internal medicine while cardiology holds spare beds for level-1 patients.

Level 2 is 2 in cardiology, 5 in internal medicine, 5 in neurology and 3 in orthopedics, 15 in total. Level 1 is 2 in cardiology, 3 in internal medicine and 4 in orthopedics. N1 requirement is 12, 13, 10 and 6 (41 in total) against 37 nurses. Maximum beds per department is 40.
explanation.alternatives: A) Keep the current allocation (beds 26/28/17/15, nurses 12/11/9/5). Result: 4 level-2 patients wait (internal medicine 1, neurology 3) while 2 level-1 patients are served in cardiology, which is a priority violation. Neurology level-2 nursing is short by 0.65. B) Proposed beds 24/29/20/13 with nurses 12/12/9/4. Result: 1 level-2 patient waits, and neurology level-2 nursing is short by 0.65. C) Chosen beds 24/29/20/13 with nurses 12/11/10/4. Result: all level-3 patients are bedded, 14 of 15 level-2 patients are bedded, and no level-3 or level-2 nursing shortage remains.
explanation.reasons: Priority: the 3 level-3 patients and 14 level-2 patients get beds before any level-1 patient. Nurses cover level 3 and level 2 fully in every department. The only uncovered nursing is level-1 (internal medicine 1.15, orthopedics 1.45). Fairness: every waiting patient has 0 days waiting, so the choice of which single level-2 patient waits is a tie. I left it in orthopedics, the department with the lowest nurse requirement. Efficiency: no bed is left empty and no nurse is idle.
explanation.tradeoffs: Beds moved: cardiology -2, internal medicine +1, neurology +3, orthopedics -2 versus the current allocation. Nurses moved: internal medicine 0, neurology +1, orthopedics -1, cardiology 0. One level-2 patient (P000996, orthopedics) waits, because the 86-bed pool cannot hold all 15. Nine level-1 patients wait, and level-1 nursing is short. This is accepted because higher levels take priority.
explanation.uncertainty: The choice of which level-2 patient waits is arbitrary because all arrived today. Tomorrow's arrivals and discharges are unknown, and recent arrivals are above their long-run mean in every department, so the demand pattern may shift. Today's reallocation may need partial reversal.
